content: Ingrown hair is a condition in which a hair curls back or grows sideways into the skin. This condition may or may not be associated with an infection of the hair follicle, known as folliculitis, or with the development of razor bumps, medically referred to as pseudofolliculitis barbae. Ingrown hairs are most commonly observed in areas where the skin is shaved, such as the beard, legs, or pubic region, but they can occur on any part of the body. Causes Ingrown hairs are caused by anything that results in the hair being broken off short with a sharp tip. Shaving is the primary cause, followed by wearing tight clothing. When the hair becomes embedded in the skin, it triggers a localized inflammatory response, which can sometimes be painful. This inflammatory reaction involves the release of prostanoids, which are compounds that mediate inflammation. Symptoms The appearance of a rash, characterized by reddened areas of skin. Persistent itching in the affected area. Hair that remains trapped beneath the skin despite shaving. Treatment Ingrown hairs can be manually removed using specialized tweezers designed for this purpose. Shaving in a different direction can help reduce the likelihood of ingrown hairs. Allowing the hair to grow out naturally can encourage it to emerge straighter from the skin. Using razors specifically designed to leave the hair slightly longer can minimize the risk of ingrown hairs. Regular exfoliation with facial scrubs, sponges, towels, or creams containing exfoliating acids can help prevent and treat ingrown hairs. For stubborn cases, treatment with ibuprofen or other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) can promote resolution of inflammation. Preventative measures include the twice-daily application of diluted glycolic acid to the affected area. Ensuring that both the skin and the razor are sterile before shaving is critical in preventing ingrown hairs. If the affected area becomes infected, it is essential to consult a dermatologist for appropriate medical management.
